2025_26|HB 1009.text: Mandates that Georgia public schools and local school systems implement policies to restrict student access to personal electronic devices during the school day to foster a 'distraction-free education'. K-8 Students: Access must be prohibited during the school day no later than July 1, 2026. High School (Grades 9-12): Access must be prohibited no later than July 1, 2027. Local systems must adopt and revise their specific policies and procedures by January 1 of each year, beginning in 2026.

2025_26|HB 103.text: The bill would increase the homestead exemption and raise the income cap for certain residents of Troup County's school district who are 65 years of age or older and have incomes not exceeding $22,000.

2025_26|HB 104.text: This bill would enact the "Equal Athletic Opportunities Act" in Georgia's school code. It would require school teams to be designated male, female, or coed, and bar males from female teams and females from male teams. It defines "sex" as biological sex based on reproductive biology and genetics at birth, which a birth certificate issued near birth can show. It applies to school systems, public schools, and private schools that compete against them.

2025_26|HB 108.text: The bill would provide protections for veterans and other eligible persons applying for benefits under the Fair Business Practices Act of 1975. It also includes provisions for violations and sets a short title for the act.

2025_26|HB 1092.text: This bill extends the life of the Chehaw Park Authority, a local authority created by a 1979 law. Under the bill, the authority would continue to exist through December 31, 2036.

2025_26|HB 111.text: Reduces Georgia's flat personal income tax rate from 5.39% to 5.19%, retroactive to January 1, 2025. Sets automatic annual 0.10% cuts until the rate reaches 4.99% — continuing Georgia's multi-year shift to a flat tax structure.

2025_26|HB 112.text: Authorizes a one-time income tax rebate of approximately $1 billion — up to $500 for married couples filing jointly, $375 for head of household, and $250 for single filers. Georgia's third consecutive year returning surplus funds to taxpayers.

2025_26|HB 1122.text: Starting January 1, 2027, this bill would require health insurance plans, the state health benefit plan, and Medicaid to cover a peripheral artery disease screening test at least once every 12 months for people at higher risk, such as those 65 or older. Coverage would follow each plan's usual deductibles and copays. The state plan and Medicaid parts take effect only if funds are appropriated.

2025_26|HB 1155.text: This bill changes how Tift County's board of commissioners handles purchasing. The board is the county's purchasing agent. Purchasing and bidding would follow a policy the board adopts, replacing the current provisions in the county's 1917 act.

2025_26|HB 1193.text: Comprehensive legislative effort to advance statewide literacy through evidence-based instruction aligned with the science of reading. The state will provide grants to fund one literacy coach per eligible school (K-3) to provide onsite, nonevaluative professional learning and side-by-side classroom support. All early literacy instruction must be focused on structured literacy and foundational skills, anchored by high-quality materials aligned with the science of reading. Local systems must annually certify that their instructional materials are high-quality and aligned with state standards.

2025_26|HB 1203.text: This bill changes how Chatham County homeowners get a school district property tax exemption created by a 2025 law. Anyone who, as of December 31, 2026, has applied for and is eligible for the existing 1999 homestead exemption from Chatham County and City of Savannah school district taxes would automatically qualify for the 2025 exemption. They would not need to apply separately.

2025_26|HB 1241.text: This bill changes the charter of the City of Decatur, rewriting the article on the city commission. The city commission has four commissioners and a mayor. Commissioners come from two election districts, and the mayor is elected citywide. Other parts of the article cover who can run for office, how terms are staggered, and how the mayor and the commission operate.

2025_26|HB 1338.text: This bill would change a 1999 homestead exemption from City of Savannah property taxes for city purposes. It would cap the "adjusted base year assessed value" of a homestead at its tax year 2025 level for later years. It would take effect only if Savannah voters approve it in the November 2026 election and the General Assembly passes it by a two-thirds vote.

2025_26|HB 134.text: This bill, the "Keep Georgia Forested Act," adds forestry manufacturers to the businesses that can earn Georgia income tax credits tied to new jobs. These are businesses certified as using wood fiber or other forest-derived materials to make products such as fuels or chemicals. For tax years 2026 through 2030, they can earn a $500 credit per new job and may sell or transfer unused credits, with reporting to the state.

2025_26|HB 1357.text: This bill changes the law that created the Bulloch County Public Facilities Authority. It revises what counts as a "project" the authority can fund with revenue bonds, including county buildings, facilities, and equipment. It bars the authority from issuing bonds for projects of the school district or other local governments in the county, and says no bond may have a maturity over 40 years.

2025_26|HB 1460.text: This bill changes how salaries are set for prosecutors in Muscogee County's State Court. The solicitor-general's pay would be at least 90 percent of a junior judge's salary in that court. The chief assistant solicitor-general would earn at least 80 percent of the solicitor-general's pay. Other assistant solicitors-general would have pay set by the solicitor-general, in line with other county or state attorneys.

2025_26|HB 1500.text: This bill changes the city limits of Suwanee in Gwinnett County. It adds about 93 acres to the city, including parcels and the unincorporated parts of McGinnis Ferry Road. It also removes about 8 acres, including a parcel and the nearby right-of-way along McGinnis Ferry Road and I-85.

2025_26|HB 1537.text: This bill would give Bibb County school district homeowners age 65 and older a homestead exemption from school district property taxes. Ages 65 to 74 would get $17,000 off the assessed value, ages 75 to 84 would get $32,000, and those 85 and older would be fully exempt. Residents must apply to the county tax commissioner. It takes effect only if Bibb County school district voters approve it in the November 2026 election.

2025_26|HB 1550.text: This bill adds an area to the City of Byron's corporate limits. The added area runs along Housers Mill Road, near the Georgia Highway 247 connector. It takes effect June 1, 2026 only if a separate act removes the same right of way from the City of Fort Valley. Otherwise, it does not take effect and is repealed that day.

2025_26|HB 1562.text: This bill would raise the homestead exemption from Pike County property taxes for totally disabled residents, from the county's 2002 law. The base exemption would be $15,000 of assessed value. Higher amounts, up to $30,000, would apply to those age 70 or older who have lived in the county for set lengths of time. It would take effect only if Pike County voters approve it in November 2026.

2025_26|HB 157.text: This bill would add certain properties in Jackson County to the Town of Braselton. The land is described by survey and plat records, with two tax parcels excluded. The change amends the town's 2003 charter so those properties fall within the town limits. It takes effect when the Governor approves it or it becomes law without approval.

2025_26|HB 1571.text: This bill changes when the State Court of Bryan County, formerly the City Court of Pembroke, holds its terms. Criminal trials would be held in four regular terms a year, starting January 2 and the first day of April, July, and October. Civil trials would be held monthly, starting on the first of each month. It takes effect July 1, 2026.

2025_26|HB 1578.text: This bill updates the charter of the Town of Arcade. It changes the municipality's name to the "City of Arcade" throughout the charter and sets the council's organizational meeting for the second Monday of January after an election. It also revises rules for emergency ordinances and gives the mayor the power to veto council actions, which the council can override by a vote of four members.

2025_26|HB 1594.text: This bill would add about 809 acres to the City of Riceboro by revising its corporate limits. The new area is described by boundary measurements that begin at the intersection of U.S. Highway 17 (South Coastal Highway) and Retreat Road. It amends the city's 1992 charter.

2025_26|HB 162.text: The bill would restrict and seal sentences for people under the First Offender Act until their status is revoked.

2025_26|HB 169.text: This bill would limit the exceptions to breaking a conservation-use covenant for solar energy generation so they apply only to existing contracts. The covenant rules are part of Georgia's property tax law for land kept in bona fide conservation use and forest land conservation use. The bill also sets a date on which these provisions end and addresses when the change applies.

2025_26|HB 170.text: The bill would require insurance benefit providers to disclose certain payments to treating healthcare providers. It also provides definitions and related matters.

2025_26|HB 176.text: The bill would change the laws about which judgments can be appealed directly and the procedures for certain types of post-judgment relief in criminal cases.

2025_26|HB 180.text: This bill changes the rules for probate court judges in Georgia counties with a population over 90,000. Candidates must be at least 30, be a member in good standing of the State Bar, and have been admitted to practice law for seven years before the election. They must also file a sworn statement saying they meet these rules. Judges already in office on or after June 30, 2000, may stay and run again.

2025_26|HB 183.text: This bill would allow innkeepers to remove and hold a guest's property after the guest leaves, as part of the innkeeper's lien rights. It also provides procedures for innkeepers to remove guests and for law enforcement to assist in such removals.

2025_26|HB 187.text: This bill creates rules for vehicle value protection agreements, optional contracts sold to car buyers that provide a benefit toward a replacement vehicle if the covered vehicle is damaged, totaled, or stolen. Providers must disclose key terms, give at least a 30-day cancellation period with refunds, and meet financial-security requirements. A vehicle loan or purchase cannot require the agreement. The Attorney General can enforce the rules and seek civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation.

2025_26|HB 189.text: This bill adds a new rule for Georgia notaries public. A notary's commission would not allow them to give legal advice, draft legal documents, act as an immigration consultant, represent anyone in immigration cases, charge for those services, or make certified copies of public records. Notaries also could not advertise falsely, sign a certificate they know is false, or hold back a person's original records. Non-attorney notaries could not use the term "notario."

2025_26|HB 198.text: The bill would allow certain youth groups designated as "patriotic society" by US Code Title 36, to use school facilities. If a local school system denies the use of facilities by a patriotic society, the principal of the school shall provide reasons in writing for the denial to the requesting entity.

2025_26|HB 207.text: This bill changes Georgia's weapons law so that a lawful weapons carrier may transport a handgun or long gun in a private passenger vehicle only in a locked compartment, a locked container, or a locked firearms rack on the vehicle. In a private vessel, it must be in a locked compartment or locked container. Violating the vehicle rule would count as unlawful carrying of a weapon. It also updates school safety zone exceptions to refer to this storage rule.

2025_26|HB 208.text: The bill would create special license plates that support organizations such as the Department of Natural Resources, Shepherd Center, Southern University Alumni, and others. Additionally it provides for the issuance of two free license plates for veterans who are totally disabled or disabled.

2025_26|HB 211.text: The bill would provide immunity from certain lawsuits related to specific chemicals for entities involved in the chemicals' handling or disposal.

2025_26|HB 215.text: The bill would remove the Secretary of State's authorization to be part of a nongovernmental group that shares and exchanges information to improve voter registration accuracy and efficiency. It also maintains an exemption for certain document disclosures and prohibits the Secretary of State from engaging in certain activities.

2025_26|HB 216.text: The bill would create a new commission called the Georgia CHIPS and Advanced Technology Commission within the Department of Economic Development. It would also abolish the Georgia CHIPS and Advanced Technology Consortium and replace its advisory panel and executive committee.

2025_26|HB 220.text: House Bill 220 changes a Georgia law about how auto insurers pay for damage to a third party's car. When an insurer under a liability policy pays for that damage, it would pay both the third party and the senior lienholder of record, if there is one, as their interests appear. If the insurer prepares the loss estimate in Georgia, the estimate must carry a printed warning about misusing the insurance money. It would apply to policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2025.

2025_26|HB 226.text: This bill adds a stretch of road to the City of Cochran's corporate limits. The added area is the right of way of State Route 23 (also U.S. Highway 87), running north from the current city limits to where it meets Jac Arts Road.

2025_26|HB 227.text: The bill would rename low THC oil as medical cannabis and clarify and revise criminal penalties related to offenses against public health and morals, regulation of controlled substances, and general provisions relative to the Department of Public Health.

2025_26|HB 240.text: The bill would prohibit unfair or deceptive practices by mortgage lenders and brokers related to mortgage trigger leads in consumer transactions.

2025_26|HB 243.text: The bill would revise the purpose of the Stone Mountain Memorial Association. It affects the association and related matters.

2025_26|HB 247.text: This bill changes Georgia's rules for DUI risk reduction programs and defensive driving courses used to restore licenses. Written consent for releasing a program participant's records could be obtained and transferred electronically. It also raises fees: defensive driving courses from $95 to $125, assessments from $100 to $150, and the intervention component from $235 to $350.

2025_26|HB 249.text: This bill changes Georgia's rules for solar power facility leases between landowners and the companies that operate the solar facilities. It requires the operator to remove equipment, including buried foundations and cables to at least three feet deep, and to provide financial assurance, such as a surety bond, to cover removal costs. It lets landowners and operators change some lease terms in a written, notarized agreement, but not the duty to remove the equipment. It also lets the Environmental Protection Division issue cease and desist orders and civil penalties.

2025_26|HB 253.text: HB 253, known as Ethan's Law, bars a judge in a child custody case from ordering family reunification programs that require no contact between a child and a parent or guardian, break a no-contact court order, use private transporters who use force or put the child at risk, or involve an out-of-state stay. It also lets ambulance services accept newborns left under Georgia's Safe Place for Newborns law and lets facilities install monitored newborn safety devices.

2025_26|HB 265.text: The bill would set limits on the amount of THC and other intoxicating cannabinoids in consumable hemp products. It would also revise the certificate of analysis for these products and establish criminal penalties.

2025_26|HB 268.text: The bill would create an Office of Safe Schools within the Georgia Emergency Management and Homeland Security Agency and provide technical assistance for local school systems to develop policies and procedures for their threat management teams.

2025_26|HB 271.text: House Bill 271 changes the definition of "agency" in Georgia's general revenue and taxation law (Code Section 48-1-2). Under the revised definition, an agency means any department, commission, institution, office, or officer of the state. The bill takes effect when the Governor approves it or it becomes law without approval.

2025_26|HB 272.text: The bill would change certain provisions regarding definitions in Georgia's revenue and taxation laws.

2025_26|HB 273.text: The bill would change certain definitions related to title ad valorem tax on motor vehicles. It adds "Immediate family member as spouse, parent, child, sibling, grandparent, or grandchild."

2025_26|HB 274.text: The bill would change certain definitions related to the alternative ad valorem tax on motor vehicles.

2025_26|HB 275.text: This version of the bill deals with property taxes, not income taxes. It lets the state revenue commissioner accept a county's tax digest if a newspaper publication error was not the county's fault. It changes what property tax bills and annual assessment notices must show, including a bold notice from local governments that opted out of HB 581 homestead relief. It also repeals the yearly estimated roll-back rate certification.

2025_26|HB 276.text: This bill creates a state income tax credit for buying, installing, and preparing a power generator that runs on woody biomass (such as land-clearing residue and wood pellets) and has at least 50 megawatts of capacity. It also changes a sales tax exemption on computer equipment for high-technology companies and data centers, adding companies that use such generators on site to those eligible from 2029 through 2034.

2025_26|HB 277.text: The bill would change certain definitions related to the excise tax on rooms, lodgings, and accommodations.

2025_26|HB 278.text: The bill would change certain definitions related to the excise tax on rooms, lodgings, and accommodations.

2025_26|HB 279.text: The bill would change certain definitions related to sales and use taxes.

2025_26|HB 280.text: The bill would change certain definitions related to sales and use taxes.

2025_26|HB 281.text: The bill would change certain definitions related to ad valorem taxation of property.

2025_26|HB 282.text: The bill revises Chapter 5, Tital 48, of the Official Code of Georgia Annotated relating to ad valorem taxation of property. Specifically, it amends the definition of "current use value" of bona fide conservation use property.

2025_26|HB 285.text: The bill would create a judicial procedure for removing a person's involuntary hospitalization information from law enforcement databases.

2025_26|HB 288.text: This bill requires a prosecutor who puts a peace officer on a "Giglio list" (officers whose credibility is in question as trial witnesses) to send written notice to the officer's employer and the state's Peace Officer Standards and Training Council. The officer or employer may ask for reconsideration within 30 days. It also requires sheriff candidates to be certified peace officers, with a six-month window after taking office for some candidates, such as former law enforcement officers, to certify.

2025_26|HB 295.text: This bill lets Georgia owners of real property submit a written claim to their city or county for money if a local government's policy or a public nuisance it maintains cuts the property's value or causes the owner expenses. Covered policies include not following immigration sanctuary and lawful-presence laws, or not enforcing laws on things like illegal camping, loitering, and shoplifting. If the claim is rejected or ignored for 30 days, the owner may sue.

2025_26|HB 305.text: The bill would prohibit certain entities from acquiring an interest in a single-family dwelling. It also provides definitions and a short title for the act.

2025_26|HB 325.text: The bill would revise certain definitions related to protective orders and military judges' processes for issuing protective orders involving members of the state militia.

2025_26|HB 327.text: This bill updates Georgia laws on trusts, estates, and family matters. It sets rules for trust directors, trustees, and estate representatives, and it covers how children born outside marriage or through assisted reproduction are treated for inheritance, parental rights, and wrongful death claims. It also raises the amount of money probate courts can distribute in cases involving minors and incapacitated people.

2025_26|HB 331.text: House Bill 331 would make it unlawful to sell, trade, or otherwise exchange a dog, cat, or domestic rabbit for something of value at roadsides, parking lots, parks, fairs, flea markets, and similar outdoor locations. Exceptions include licensed animal shelters, transfers at a home or inside a business, certain breed or 4-H shows, and prearranged transfers at law enforcement facilities. Officers may impound animals and enforce the law. Fines are up to $100, $250, then $500 for repeat violations.

2025_26|HB 335.text: The bill would amend the Quality Basic Education Act to address mental health risks for student athletes by providing guidelines and materials to educate athletes, their parents or guardians, school personnel, and coaches about mental health risks and raise awareness of mental health resources.

2025_26|HB 349.text: The bill would change the provisions for filling vacancies on the Board of Commissioners of Douglas County.

2025_26|HB 351.text: The bill would change the powers and duties of the Board of Natural Resources, revise definitions, and modify solid waste permitting requirements. It also requires written verification of compliance with local zoning and land use regulations.

2025_26|HB 353.text: The bill would create the Georgia Music Office and set out its duties. It would also provide for the adoption and promulgation of rules and regulations by the office.

2025_26|HB 358.text: The bill would amend a law to add a definition related to prohibiting foreign persons and entities from acquiring certain land in Georgia. Specifically, it adds "Military Installation" as a new definition.

2025_26|HB 382.text:
The bill would revise a provision in Georgia law related to Schedule I controlled substances, specifically regarding crystalline polymorph
psilocybin and lysergide tartrate.

2025_26|HB 391.text: This bill updates Georgia's rules for boxing, wrestling, and martial arts events. It changes the definition of an "amateur" and the list of organizations whose events are exempt from the state's regulation of these sports. The list drops the International Sport Combat Federation and the International Kick Boxing Federation. It keeps the rest, including USA Wrestling and the Georgia High School Athletic Association, and the Professional Karate Commission stays on it.

2025_26|HB 400.text: The bill would allow certain local governments to seek certifications from the Department of Community Affairs if they enact specific policies. These certifications could help these local governments get priority in grant and loan applications submitted to state agencies.

2025_26|HB 403.text: The bill aims to enhance protections for homeowners and tenants by revising or removing certain provisions that hinder housing stability.

2025_26|HB 404.text: This bill changes the boundaries of the City of Conyers. It adds nine listed properties, mostly along Milstead Avenue (Highway 20) and one on Old Covington Highway, in Rockdale County, to the city limits. Each parcel is described by its address and legal land description.

2025_26|HB 412.text: This bill changes the rules for how long members of the Polk County Water Authority can serve. A member cannot be reappointed for two years after the end of their second consecutive term. Members also keep serving until their successors are appointed and qualified.

2025_26|HB 44.text: This bill would establish protections for consumers who use self-service storage facilities. It sets requirements for the owners of these facilities and rental agreements. It also defines what actions are considered unfair or deceptive trade practices.

2025_26|HB 468.text: This bill changes how members of the Heard County Board of Education are paid. Each member would receive $450 per month. Members who travel outside the county on board business, such as for training or state meetings, would be reimbursed for actual expenses if a majority of the board approves the travel first. The change takes effect July 1, 2025.

2025_26|HB 514.text: This bill adds a described 2.20-acre parcel in Land Lot 208 of Cobb County, near Ernest Barrett Parkway and U.S. Highway 41, to the corporate limits of the City of Kennesaw. It amends the city's 2013 charter to do so.

2025_26|HB 53.text: This bill would allow certain individuals to be buried in Georgia veterans cemeteries. It also provides for definitions, fees, and legislative findings.

2025_26|HB 548.text: This bill rewrites the 1977 law that created the Albany-Dougherty Inner City Authority, a public body serving the City of Albany and Dougherty County. It gives the law a short title and restates the authority's definitions, purposes, and membership. The authority can own, sell, or lease projects, including redevelopment projects, and the bill also covers revenue bonds, immunity, and tax exemptions.

2025_26|HB 598.text: This bill would create the "Reproductive Freedom Act" and state that every individual has a fundamental right to reproductive freedom. It would repeal Georgia's criminal abortion provisions and the "Woman's Right to Know Act." It would change the Parental Notification Act for minors seeking abortions and add exceptions to its notice rules. It would also remove limits on insurance and Medicaid coverage of abortion.

2025_26|HB 6.text: This bill changes how vacancies on the Mitchell County Board of Commissioners are filled, unless the vacancy comes from a term expiring. If a seat opens in the first 21 months of a term, the board directs the county election superintendent to call a special election, and the chief judge of the judicial circuit appoints someone to serve until it is held. If a seat opens in the last 27 months, the chief judge appoints a person to serve out the term.

2025_26|HB 622.text: This bill changes how much the mayor and city council members of Hoboken, Georgia are paid. The mayor would receive $475 per month, and each councilmember would receive $175 per month. They would also be repaid for actual and necessary expenses they have while doing their jobs.

2025_26|HB 67.text: This bill would amend the General Appropriations Act for the State Fiscal Year starting July 1, 2024, and ending June 30, 2025, to make changes to the state's budget for various government departments, boards, commissions, institutions, and other agencies, as well as for the university system, common schools, counties, municipalities, and other entities.

2025_26|HB 68.text: FY 2026 state appropriations budget ($37.7 billion). Funds K–12 education, corrections, healthcare, and Hurricane Helene recovery. Includes $141 million to launch the Georgia Promise Scholarship (school voucher) program.

2025_26|HB 69.text: This bill would amend the General Appropriations Act for the State Fiscal Year beginning July 1, 2024, and ending June 30, 2025, to make, provide, and change certain appropriations for the operation of the state government and its departments, boards, bureaus, commissions, institutions, and other agencies, as well as for the university system, common schools, counties, municipalities, and political subdivisions.

2025_26|HB 698.text: This bill would give some Walker County school district homeowners a break on school property taxes. Residents 70 and older would get a $50,000 homestead exemption. Residents 75 and older who have lived in the district five years or more would be exempt on the full assessed value of their homestead. Voters in the district would decide in November 2026.

2025_26|HB 70.text: HB 70 would amend the General Appropriations Act for the State Fiscal Year starting July 1, 2024, to make changes in funding for state government operations, departments, boards, and other agencies, as well as for the university system, common schools, counties, and municipalities.

2025_26|HB 71.text: HB 71 would provide appropriations for the State Fiscal Year starting July 1, 2025, and ending June 30, 2026, covering various state government operations, departments, and agencies, as well as educational and local government activities.

2025_26|HB 719.text: This bill changes how much Worth County board of education members are paid. The chairperson would receive $300 per day and each other member $200 per day for attending board meetings or committee meetings and travel on official board business approved in advance by a majority of the board. Actual expenses would also be reimbursed. It takes effect on the first day of the month after it becomes law.

2025_26|HB 74.text: This bill changes how the Georgia Administrative Procedure Act applies to the Georgia Lottery Corporation. Rules, licensing, and hearings for licensees under Article 3 of the lottery law, which covers bona fide coin operated amusement machines, would follow that Act. Other lottery rules stay exempt, and hearings under Code Section 50-27-102 would follow the Georgia Arbitration Code. It also corrects a reference.

2025_26|HB 76.text: This bill would require the Georgia Department of Transportation to hold public hearings for "local transportation projects of significant impact." These are road or other transportation projects the department helps with for a county, city, or private group that make major changes, such as new roads, extensions, or a rebuilt major intersection. The hearings would follow rules similar to those for the department's other planning hearings.

2025_26|HB 771.text: This bill would change a Cherokee County School District property tax exemption for residents who are disabled or at least 62 and meet an income limit. It would waive the five-year homestead requirement for the surviving spouse of someone who got the exemption. It would take effect only if Cherokee County school district voters approve it in an election no later than November 2026.

2025_26|HB 836.text: This bill would raise the Coweta County School District homestead exemption from school property taxes for older homeowners. The exemption would go to $75,000 of assessed value for ages 65 to 70 and $100,000 for ages 71 to 74. Residents 75 and older would be fully exempt from school taxes on their homestead. It takes effect only if Coweta County voters approve it in a November 2025 election.

2025_26|HB 842.text: This bill would raise the Whitfield County homestead exemption for residents 70 or older from $250,000 to $325,000 of appraised value, for county property taxes. It would apply to tax years starting January 1, 2026. It would take effect only if Whitfield County voters approve it in a November 2025 election.

2025_26|HB 844.text: This bill would raise a homestead exemption from Whitfield County School District property taxes for educational purposes. The exemption would go from $250,000 to $325,000 of a home's appraised value for residents of the school district who are 70 or older. It would apply to tax years beginning in 2026 and takes effect only if voters approve it in a November 2025 election.

2025_26|HB 849.text: This bill renames the Lower Chattahoochee Regional Airport Authority as the Randolph County Airport Authority. The renamed authority becomes the successor to the old one and takes over its assets, debts, and obligations. The bill also updates the authority's name in the law's short title and in the rules for validating its bonds.

2025_26|HB 859.text: If voters approve it in a November 2026 referendum, this bill would raise the Cartersville school district property tax homestead exemption for residents who are 65 or older or totally disabled. The exemption would range from $60,000 for ages 65–69 or totally disabled to $200,000 for ages 80 and up. It would apply to tax years 2028 through 2032 only.

2025_26|HB 861.text: This bill would raise the homestead exemption from City of Calhoun independent school district property taxes for older residents, if local voters approve it in a November 2025 referendum. The exemption would become $50,000 for ages 65 to 69, $115,000 for ages 70 to 74, and $125,000 for ages 75 and older. Each amount applies to the assessed value of the home.

2025_26|HB 982.text: This bill changes how the City of Barnesville's five city council districts are described, using a new map labeled "barnesville-p1-2025." The districts keep their numbers (1 through 5). Current council members stay in office until their terms end and are treated as serving from the newly described districts. It affects voters and council members in Barnesville.

2025_26|HR 119.text: This resolution directs the Department of Administrative Services to pay Mario Stinchcomb $975,000 for his wrongful murder conviction, for which he was exonerated in 2021. He would get an initial $321,750, with the rest paid in monthly installments over ten years starting in 2026. The state would get a credit for any damages he wins in a related lawsuit, and the payment would be excluded from his state taxable income.

2025_26|SB 116.text: The bill requires DNA samples to be collected via oral swab or other noninvasive procedures from individuals charged with a misdemeanor or felony who are also subject to an immigration detainer notice. This requirement applies if the individual is not taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) within 48 hours of detention, excluding weekends and holidays. Samples must be collected by the detention facility (such as county jails, municipal facilities, or state prisons) detaining the individual or the entity supervising them.

2025_26|SB 189.text: This bill would have the Department of Community Affairs build and run a free-to-search public website of legal notices that the law now requires to be published in a newspaper. It would depend on funding from the General Assembly. Posting on the site would be required in addition to newspaper publication. In some cases, such as when a county's legal newspaper has no local office, a posting could replace newspaper publication.

2025_26|SB 233.text: This bill changes the Behavioral Health Reform and Innovation Commission. It raises the commission from 24 to 30 members and adds seats such as people with lived experience of addiction or overdose loss and disability-related roles. It renames the subcommittees, replacing two with Addictive Diseases and Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities. It also moves the commission's end date from June 30, 2025, to December 31, 2026.

2025_26|SB 346.text: This bill changes how DeKalb County pays certain officials. It sets the salaries of the CEO, sheriff, clerk of superior court, tax commissioner, and county commissioners as percentages of a "gross salary" figure. Judges of the State, Juvenile, and Probate Courts, the chief magistrate, and the solicitor-general get the higher of $208,040 or 90 percent of that figure. It also sets associate magistrate pay and renames the Stone Mountain Judicial Circuit the DeKalb Judicial Circuit.

2025_26|SB 348.text: This bill changes how Hancock County's four commissioner districts are described, using a new map named in the bill. The chairperson is still elected by the whole county. Current commissioners stay in office until their terms end, and districts 1 through 4 keep their numbers under the new descriptions. The bill takes effect July 1, 2025.

2025_26|SB 350.text: This bill changes how much certain DeKalb County officials and judges are paid. It sets salaries for officials such as the Chief Executive Officer, District Attorney, Sheriff, Clerk of the Superior Court, Tax Commissioner, and county commissioners as percentages of a base "gross salary." It also sets pay for several judges, the Chief Magistrate, and the Solicitor-General, and for associate magistrates. It updates references to the Stone Mountain Judicial Circuit, now called the DeKalb Judicial Circuit.

2025_26|SB 443.text: The bill defines the legal consequences for individuals who, without legal authority, purposely or recklessly obstruct a public passage so that it becomes impassable without 'unreasonable inconvenience or hazard' and refuse to move after an official request. A significant addition in this bill is the introduction of civil consequences. Beyond criminal fines, penalties, or restitution, a person found guilty of this offense can be held civilly liable for damages resulting from the obstruction.

2025_26|SB 609.text: This bill removes one residential property, at 1195 University Drive, NE, Atlanta, from the DeKalb County school district. The property would instead become part of the Atlanta Independent School System. It amends the law that sets up DeKalb County Board of Education districts and affects the students and residents of that address.

2025_26|SB 623.text: This bill changes how the solicitor-general of the State Court of Clayton County is paid. The salary would equal 95 percent of the Chief Judge of that court's total compensation, including any supplements, paid from Clayton County funds. The salary could not exceed the greater of $191,007 or that 95 percent figure. The change takes effect only after the solicitor-general complies with required county audits for 2024, 2025, and 2026.

2026_ss|SR 3EX.text: This Senate resolution sets the meeting schedule for the 2026 special session of the General Assembly from June 17 to June 22, 2026. It lists Special Session Days 1 through 4 on June 17, 18, 20 and 22, with no meetings on June 19 and 21. After June 22, adjournments follow later resolutions, and the General Assembly stays adjourned on Saturdays and Sundays unless another resolution says otherwise. It also lets the House Speaker and Senate President jointly move meetings during an emergency or disaster.

2025_26|SR 4.text: This Senate resolution sets how the Senate runs for the 2025-2026 term. It lets the Senate Committee on Administrative Affairs, the Secretary of the Senate, and the President of the Senate hire staff and set their pay within available funds. It also lets senators claim expense, mileage, and travel allowances for official days when the General Assembly is not in session, with limits set by the committee. The Majority and Minority Leaders get extra annual salary of $2,400.

2025_26|SR 424.text: This resolution creates a five-member Senate study committee on franchise fees. Franchise fees are what electric utilities pay cities to use public rights of way; the resolution says people in unincorporated areas pay these city fees through their electric bills, and that counties get no similar payment. The committee will study how these fees are assessed and divided, including for large electricity customers in unincorporated areas, and may recommend legislation. It ends December 1, 2025.

2025_26|SR 890.text: This resolution creates the Senate Study Committee on Protecting Free and Fair Markets in Georgia, made up of five senators appointed by the President of the Senate. The committee will study Georgia's antitrust laws and enforcement, how concentrated economic power affects housing, technology, agriculture, healthcare, and retail, and how other states handle antitrust and merger review. It will also look at possible changes to protect consumers and small businesses. The committee ends December 1, 2026.

2023_24|SB 233.text: Georgia Promise Scholarship Act. Allows families of students in the lowest-performing 25% of public schools to receive up to $6,500 in state funds for private school tuition or homeschooling. Passed the House 91–82, largely along party lines. Program launched Fall 2025.

2023_24|SB 189.text: Amends Georgia election law: defines grounds for challenging voter eligibility (death, out-of-state registration, non-residential address), requires counties to report absentee ballot results within one hour of polls closing, and restricts non-citizens from employment in county election offices.
